strengths: The paper addresses a very practical and relevant problem in autonomous driving: bridging local online HD map perception with global SD map navigation (hybrid navigation).

The proposed Online Map Association (OMA) benchmark builds upon popular public datasets (nuScenes and OpenStreetMap) and considers both ground truth HD map inputs (OMA-GT) and noisy online predicted HD map inputs (OMA from MapTRv2).

The Map Association Transformer (MAT) architecture sensibly incorporates both topological path structure (Path-Aware Attention) and geometric spatial proximity (Spatial Attention via space-filling curves and RoPE).
The paper includes detailed ablation studies examining the contribution of individual attention mechanisms, losses (CE vs. CTC), and grouping strategies.
weaknesses: Severe drafting and formatting issues throughout the manuscript: the abstract ends with an incomplete sentence ('The code and dataset can be accessed at'), and the entire References section is duplicated verbatim (pages 10–12 and pages 12–14).

Internal inconsistencies in experimental details: Section 6.1 reports a learning rate of 0.0001, weight decay 0.05, and batch size 128, whereas Section F.2 reports a base learning rate of 2e-3, weight decay 5e-3, and mini-batch size of 12 (though Table 9 lists batch size 128 and lr 1e-5). These conflicting figures hurt reproducibility.

Potential data labeling circularity: Section 4.1 states that 'An automated labeling pipeline using a Map Association Transformer (MAT, Section 5) trained on proprietary Chinese HD-SD maps generates initial annotations on nuScenes, followed by topological post-processing' and manual refinement. Using MAT to pre-annotate the benchmark on which MAT is subsequently evaluated risks architectural and systematic bias in favor of the proposed model.

Weak and limited baseline comparisons: The only compared baselines are basic non-learning heuristics (KNN) and classical probabilistic map-matching (HMM). The evaluation lacks modern learning-based baselines, such as standard Cross-Attention Transformers, Graph Neural Networks (e.g., GCN/GAT matching), or VectorNet-style architectures adapted for graph/vector association.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical problem in autonomous driving: bridging the gap between local online HD maps generated by perception systems and global SD maps used for route navigation.
The formulation of the Online Map Association (OMA) benchmark combining nuScenes and OpenStreetMap provides a structured testbed for cross-map topological association.

The proposed Map Association Transformer (MAT) leverages sound architectural concepts, incorporating path-aware and serialized spatial attention mechanisms to model both geometric proximities and topological sequences.
weaknesses: Severe manuscript preparation and formatting defects: the abstract ends mid-sentence ('The code and dataset can be accessed at'), and the bibliography is erroneously duplicated multiple times across pages 10–14, resulting in duplicate entries and orphan pages.

Notable internal inconsistencies in numbers and experimental configurations: Section 6.1 lists a learning rate of 1e-4, weight decay of 0.05, and batch size of 128, whereas Section F.2 / Table 9 reports a base learning rate of 2e-3 (or 1e-5), weight decay of 5e-3, and mini-batch size of 12. Furthermore, Section 7 claims an A-F1 score of 32.3% on OMA (+5.5% over HMM), which directly contradicts Table 1 where MAT reports 42.3% (+6.3% over HMM).

Extremely weak and outdated baseline comparisons: the method is only compared against a basic KNN heuristic and a standard 2009 HMM map matcher. There is an absence of competitive modern deep learning baselines, such as graph neural network matching models, learned point/vector cross-attention architectures, or trajectory-to-map alignment frameworks.

Lack of downstream impact evaluation: while the motivation is driving by hybrid navigation, the paper evaluates only intermediate classification/overlap metrics (A-P/R) without demonstrating whether or how the predicted association improves downstream motion planning, route execution, or trajectory forecasting.

Frequent typographical and terminological errors throughout the manuscript (e.g., repeated spelling of beam search as 'beem search' on pages 8, 18, and 21; 'for learn topological representations' on page 2; 'An TP' on page 5).

strengths: Important and practical problem: Bridging online perception-based HD maps (which have limited local ranges) with global SD maps (such as OpenStreetMap) is a critical and under-explored step toward real-world navigation in autonomous driving.

Benchmark contribution: Introduces the Online Map Association (OMA) dataset built on nuScenes and OpenStreetMap with both predicted HD maps (OMA) and ground truth HD maps (OMA-GT), accompanied by a tailored evaluation metric (Association P-R).

Sound methodological design: The Map Association Transformer (MAT) reasonably integrates path-aware attention for topological reasoning and space-filling curve serialization for spatial attention, paired with a hybrid CE + CTC loss and topological post-processing.

Detailed component ablations: The ablation studies systematically assess the contributions of path-aware attention, spatial attention, RoPE positional encoding, boundary vectors, and the dual loss objective.
weaknesses: Weak and limited baselines: The proposed method is compared solely against classical non-learning heuristics (KNN geometric matching and an HMM map-matching algorithm from 2009). The evaluation lacks comparisons with modern deep learning baselines, such as Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), cross-attention graph matching architectures, or Hungarian-matching-based formulations.

Unfair latency comparison: Table 1 and Table 2 compare GPU latency of MAT on an NVIDIA A6000 (70–74 ms) against unoptimized Python/NumPy implementations of KNN and HMM running on an Intel Xeon CPU (300–560 ms). As the authors note in Section 6.1, optimized C++ implementations of KNN/HMM would be orders of magnitude faster, making the current runtime comparison misleading.

No downstream validation: Although the work is strongly motivated by enabling lane-level hybrid navigation and motion planning, the empirical validation is confined strictly to association metrics without demonstrating whether or how downstream trajectory planning actually benefits from this association.

Significant editorial issues and inconsistencies: The reference list is duplicated in its entirety (references [1]–[35] appear on pages 10–12 and are repeated verbatim on pages 12–14). The abstract ends mid-sentence ('The code and dataset can be accessed at '). Key training hyperparameters are inconsistent across sections (e.g., learning rate is stated as 1e-4 in Section 6.1, 1e-5 in Table 9, and 2e-3 in Section F.2; batch size is 128 in Section 6.1/Table 9 but stated as mini-batches of size 12 in Section F.2). The conclusion reports 32.3% A-F1 on OMA, which contradicts Table 1 (42.3%).

strengths: Practical and timely problem formulation: Bridging static SD navigation maps and real-time online perception (OP) maps directly addresses the industry bottleneck of high-definition (HD) map maintenance costs and latency in autonomous navigation.

Comprehensive benchmark contribution: The release of the Online Map Association Dataset (OMA) featuring over 30K scenarios and 2.6M annotated lane vectors provides a valuable and previously missing resource for the community.

Well-motivated architecture: MAT effectively addresses computational complexity and heterogeneity by combining Path-Aware Attention (for topological ordering) and Spatial Attention via space-filling curves (for geometric locality), achieving linear computational complexity and real-time inference latency (34 ms).

Thorough experimental validation: The paper evaluates against classical and deep map matching, graph matching, and point matching baselines across three different OP map generators (MapTR, MapTRv2, SeqGrowGraph), alongside rigorous ablations covering cross-city transfer, SD map noise, weather corruptions (nuScenes-C), and data efficiency.
weaknesses: High sensitivity of the evaluation metric to upstream perception noise: In Table 19, tightening the distance threshold from 1.0 m to 0.5 m causes test performance to plummet drastically (from 45.0% to 6.6%), highlighting that the overall navigation refinement remains heavily bottlenecked by upstream perception accuracy.

Decoupled perception and association: While the modular design allows evaluating arbitrary OP map generators, the pipeline does not support gradient backpropagation into the perception backbone, missing out on potential benefits from joint end-to-end optimization.
Minor typographic and formatting errors: Minor typos exist in the text and tables (e.g., 'SeqGrowGrpah' in Table 2 caption, sporadic grammatical slips in Section 1 and Section 5).

strengths: Practical and timely problem: Fusing lightweight global SD navigation routes with real-time local online perception (OP) maps addresses a key bottleneck in 'HD-map-free' autonomous driving and navigation systems.

Comprehensive benchmark contribution: The authors introduce OMA (30K+ scenarios, 480K road paths, 2.6M lane vectors) and the Navigation Refinement Precision-Recall (NR P-R) metric, which properly handles the many-to-one and noisy nature of online perception outputs.

Effective and efficient architecture: The proposed Map Association Transformer (MAT) combines path-aware attention (topological ordering) and spatial attention (space-filling curve serialization) with group attention, achieving an attractive balance between topological/geometric awareness and real-time efficiency (34 ms latency).

Thorough empirical evaluation: Strong validation across clean and noisy OP inputs (generated by MapTR, MapTRv2, and SeqGrowGraph), cross-city generalization (Boston and Singapore), robustness under environmental corruptions (nuScenes-C), and detailed ablation studies.
weaknesses: Baseline comparability: As Online Navigation Refinement is newly formalized, baselines adapted from traditional map matching (path-to-map) and graph/point matching are not inherently tailored to the many-to-one heterogeneous lane-to-road formulation, giving MAT a significant structural advantage.

Lack of closed-loop downstream validation: While the paper thoroughly evaluates map association accuracy via NR P-R, it does not demonstrate end-to-end downstream planning impact (e.g., closed-loop trajectory planning metrics or intervention rates) when integrated into a planner.
Minor presentation polish: Minor typos exist in the text and tables (e.g., 'SeqGrowGrpah' in Table 2, and slightly inconsistent notation between the main text and appendix).

strengths: Practical and timely problem formulation: As autonomous driving shifts from expensive static HD maps to online perception (OP) maps, linking local perception to global standard-definition (SD) navigation routes is an important challenge bridging perception and route planning.

Dataset contribution: The authors introduce the OMA benchmark with 30K scenarios and 2.6M annotated lane-to-road vectors based on nuScenes and OpenStreetMap, providing an empirical benchmark for SD-to-OP map association.

Well-motivated architecture: The Map Association Transformer (MAT) incorporates path-aware attention and space-filling curve (Hilbert) spatial attention to preserve topological structure and spatial proximity while maintaining linear O(N) complexity and low runtime latency (34 ms).

Comprehensive experimental analysis: The evaluation covers multiple map generators (MapTR, MapTRv2, SeqGrowGraph), robustness tests under synthetic SD map shifts/omissions, and environmental corruptions (nuScenes-C).
weaknesses: Baseline suitability and fairness: Most compared baselines (e.g., HMM, DeepMM, MTrajRec, GraphMM, EAM3) are path-to-map trajectory matching algorithms designed to align 1D sequence observations to a road graph, rather than map-to-map association models. Similarly, FastMAC and GMT are generic point/graph matching methods not designed for road network primitives. The lack of stronger, competitive map-to-map or hierarchical vector-matching baselines weakens the claim of superiority.

Conflation of upstream perception errors with association performance: There is an enormous performance discrepancy between the validation set (78.7% NR-F1 using ground truth OP maps) and the test set (45.0% using MapTRv2). Because predictions with Chamfer distance > 1.0 m are automatically labeled as false positives, the test score heavily reflects upstream perception inaccuracies rather than matching capability alone.

Limited geographic and operational diversity: The OMA dataset is derived exclusively from the nuScenes scenes in Boston and Singapore within small local crops (30 m x 60 m for OP, 150 m x 150 m for SD). This scope does not adequately capture global diversity in SD map quality, complex interchanges, multi-level flyovers, or varying lane layouts.

Complexity and design choices of the evaluation metric: The proposed NR P-R metric combines multiple hand-tuned stages (point matching with a 1m Chamfer threshold, sequence traversal checking, and 15 arbitrary length-interval bins). The resulting evaluation is highly sensitive to these hyperparameter choices, making cross-method fairness difficult to guarantee.

Writing quality and presentation issues: The paper contains numerous grammatical awkwardnesses and informal phrasings (e.g., repeatedly referring to the task as a 'mission', typos like 'SeqGrowGrpah', 'Tab. 1' when referring to Table 2, and awkward phrasing such as 'The vehicle of the ego').
